page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Apply the property with a=π and add
steps.margin_note: First mark. cos⁶(π−x) stays positive because 6 is even — only cos³(π−x) or another odd power would flip sign.
steps.memory_tip: An even power of cosine is unaffected by π−x, exactly like it is unaffected by −x.
lines: I = ∫₀^π x sin⁷x cos⁶x dx = ∫₀^π (π−x) sin⁷(π−x) cos⁶(π−x) dx
sin(π−x)=sinx, cos(π−x)=−cosx ⇒ cos⁶(π−x)=cos⁶x   [even power keeps the sign positive]
∴ I = ∫₀^π (π−x) sin⁷x cos⁶x dx = π∫₀^π sin⁷x cos⁶x dx − I
steps.why: Under x→π−x, sinx is unchanged and cosx flips sign, but the even power 6 removes that sign again, so the integrand's shape sin⁷xcos⁶x survives while only the factor x turns into π−x, splitting into a constant-times-integral term minus I itself.
common_mistakes: Treating cos⁶(π−x) as −cos⁶x instead of +cos⁶x, forgetting that an even power removes the sign flip.
Losing the −I term and treating the right side as just π∫₀^π sin⁷xcos⁶x dx.

steps.label: Apply Walli's formula and solve for I
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Dividing 32π/3003 by 2 gives the final answer 16π/3003.
steps.memory_tip: The denominator product for m+n=13 has SEVEN descending terms, one more than the six-term products seen earlier in this chapter.
lines: 2I = π∫₀^π sin⁷x cos⁶x dx = 2π∫₀^(π/2) sin⁷x cos⁶x dx
steps.why: The remaining integral ∫₀^π sin⁷xcos⁶x dx is itself symmetric about π/2, so it doubles the 0-to-π/2 range; applying Walli's mixed-power formula for m=7 (odd) and n=6 (even), so K=1, and dividing the whole equation by 2 gives the final value of I.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to halve at the very last step to isolate I from 2I.
Missing a term in the seven-term denominator descending product 13·11·9·7·5·3·1.
